title: Roll-up strategy: what do holdcos actually use AI for after close?
description: What holdcos, roll-ups and independent sponsors use AI for after close, ranked by payoff. Plus the roll-up evidence, the rules and where AI roll-ups stand.
topic: AI for holding companies and roll-ups
job: running a group of acquired companies
verdict: Roll-ups win on operations: growth and margin, not resale multiples, drive returns for buy-and-build deals and serial acquirers.[^1][^2]
Acquired companies usually start with little AI: 43% of private equity (PE) portfolio companies make no real use of it.[^3][^4]
Start with shared finance and clean data, then pricing and cross-sell; front-line automation comes last.[^5][^4]
Keep acquired owners and staff: roll-ups did better when founders stayed, and acquired workers leave fast.[^6][^7]
AI roll-ups have raised billions, but their results are still unproven and mostly self-reported.[^8][^9]

summary: A roll-up strategy buys several small firms in one fragmented industry and runs them as one larger business.[^1][^6] AI changes the operating work across those firms: shared finance, clean data, pricing and cross-sell.[^5][^3] Done with the acquired teams, it drives the growth that separates winning roll-ups.[^1][^6]
humanRole: The holdco CEO owns the AI plan and its budget. In a Latin American (LATAM) survey of 10 operators, CEO-led AI work was judged worth it 4 times in 5, against 1 in 5 otherwise.[^4]

Each company's controller signs off its close and every intercompany entry, while AI drafts matches and flags differences. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI framework asks firms to name who oversees each AI system.[^10]

Each company's general manager (GM) owns pricing and customer changes, and acquired founders sit on the rollout group. Roll-ups did better when acquired owners stayed on as directors and shareholders.[^6][^11]
People make hiring, pay and discipline calls, with a documented review. Colorado's 2026 law gives people a right to request human review of adverse automated decisions, including in employment.[^12]

ranked.name: Shared finance: the group close, consolidation and intercompany entries
ranked.why: Close to half of add-ons are a platform's fourth deal or later, so each month-end spans more ledgers.[^1] Only 14% of portfolio finance functions have moved past back-office automation, operating partners say.[^5]
ranked.payoff: Days to close the group books, and intercompany differences cleared before month-end.

ranked.name: Data standards: one chart of accounts, customer list and customer relationship management (CRM) system
ranked.why: Operating partners rank data infrastructure as the top barrier to AI.[^5] In a LATAM survey of 10 operators, 7 in 10 acquired companies had no CRM.[^4]
ranked.payoff: Share of companies reporting on the same chart of accounts and customer fields.

ranked.name: Pricing, cross-sell and the sales pipeline across companies
ranked.why: Buy-and-build deals that also grew returned 2.2x, against 1.4x from reselling at a higher multiple alone.[^1] PE leaders aim AI at revenue more than cost: 41% against 24%.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Revenue from customers sold a second company's service, and win rate on quotes.

ranked.name: Integrating each new add-on
ranked.why: Integrating AI into the next acquired business is not much easier than into the last one.[^13] AI roll-up investors name integration and change management as the top risk, at 79%.[^14]
ranked.payoff: Days from close until the add-on reports in the group's format.

ranked.name: Value creation plan and board reporting
ranked.why: 44% of operating partners report AI already drafting board packages in portfolio finance teams.[^5] Only 29% of operating partners include AI's impact in board and investor reporting.[^5]
ranked.payoff: Hours to produce the monthly board pack, and plan items with a named owner and measure.

ranked.name: Deal sourcing and diligence
ranked.why: 79% of independent sponsor professionals expect AI to significantly change their model.[^15] In 161 buy-and-build buyouts, buying add-ons at lower multiples than the platform explained much of the outperformance.[^16]
ranked.payoff: Targets screened per month, and days from first look to letter of intent.

ranked.name: Training and onboarding across companies
ranked.why: In the LATAM survey of 10 operators, 7 had no AI training program.[^4] Half named onboarding and marketing as a bottleneck.[^4]
ranked.payoff: Share of staff at each company using the shared tools every week.

ranked.name: Front-line service work: tickets, tax returns, scheduling
ranked.why: Ranked last because the evidence is company-reported: Current says its tools save 31% of time across 7,000 returns.[^17] Sloppy AI output can eat the gains in services work.[^18]
ranked.payoff: Time per ticket or return, with a reviewer checking a weekly sample.

ownData.title: What do AI roll-ups prove in public about their results?
ownData.intro: On 26 Nov 2026 we read the public pages of four AI roll-ups and logged each outcome claim, such as time saved or accuracy.[^19][^17][^21][^18] For each claim we noted who reported it and whether anyone outside checked it. We name no winner: the point is the source type, not the company.
rows: Current says its tools save 31% of preparer time on average, across 7,000 tax returns.[^17]
General Catalyst relays Long Lake's figure that its top homeowners' association managers reclaim over 65 hours a month.[^19]
OpenAI, which co-built Current's tax tool with Thrive Holdings, reports about a third of time saved and up to 97% accuracy.[^20]
General Catalyst told TechCrunch that Titan's pilots showed 38% of typical managed IT service tasks could be automated.[^18]
None found. Mimetic notes even AI roll-ups' capital and deal counts are company-reported.[^8]
ownData.note: Zavient check of public company, investor and press pages, read 26 Nov 2026. Four platforms that publish outcome figures, so not a random sample, and claims change often. It logs who reports each claim and judges no company.

tables.title: Do roll-ups and serial acquirers create value?
tables.intro: Results come from public-market studies and private equity deal data.[^23][^1] Samples and periods differ, so read each row on its own terms.

rows.name: Roll-up IPOs, US
cells: Negative long-run returns, about -2.01% a month below benchmark.[^22] Better when acquired owners stayed.[^6]

rows.name: Roll-up vs build-up IPOs, US
cells: Roll-ups underperformed; build-ups matched the market.[^24]

rows.name: Serial acquirers, global
cells: 68% of deals involved a serial acquirer, and serial acquirers drove over 70% of $15T in value.[^23]

rows.name: Later deals by serial acquirers, global
cells: Announcement returns fall in later deals, mostly from the fifth deal on.[^25]

rows.name: Programmatic acquirers, global
cells: Earned 3.9% excess shareholder return over a decade.[^2]

rows.name: Buy-and-build buyouts
cells: Reselling at a higher multiple alone returned 1.4x; deals that also grew or lifted margins returned 2.2x.[^1]

rows.name: Buy-and-build buyouts, sourcing
cells: Buying add-ons at lower multiples than the platform drives a large share of returns; without it, results sit close to other buyouts.[^16]

tables.intro: Surveys of PE firms, independent sponsors and searchers, 2026.[^3][^15] Each asked different people, so compare with care.

rows.name: FTI Consulting, PE AI Radar

cells: Only 14% of portfolio finance functions have moved beyond back-office automation, operating partners say.[^5] 41% of operating partners roll AI out across companies with no playbook.[^5]

rules.name: 2023 Merger Guidelines, Guideline 8: a series of acquisitions
rules.status: In force; the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and Department of Justice (DOJ) kept them in Feb 2025
rules.what: The agencies may examine a series of small acquisitions as a whole, not one deal at a time.[^27][^29] Track your share of each local market as you add companies.

rules.name: FTC final order: Welsh Carson and U.S. Anesthesia Partners
rules.what: The FTC finalised its order against a private equity firm over its anesthesia roll-up.[^30] Treat it as a sign that repeated deals in one local market draw scrutiny.

rules.name: Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) premerger notification form
rules.status: Prior form in use; the new form was vacated 12 Feb 2026
rules.what: The expanded premerger form was vacated, a stay was denied in Mar 2026, and the FTC accepts the prior form.[^31] Check the FTC page before each filing.

rules.name: FTC: privacy promises survive an acquisition
rules.what: Privacy promises a company made to its customers still apply after you buy it.[^28] Check each company's privacy notice before you pool customer data or train AI on it.

rules.name: Colorado SB26-189, automated decisions
rules.status: Signed 14 May 2026; developer duties start 1 Jan 2027
rules.what: People get a right to request human review after an adverse automated decision, including in employment.[^12] Keep a person on hiring, pay and discipline at any Colorado company you own.

rules.name: New York City Local Law 144, automated hiring tools
rules.status: In force in New York City
rules.what: Automated hiring tools used for New York City jobs need a bias audit.[^32] Check this before you roll one screening tool out across every company.

watchOuts: Losing key people: 33% of acquired tech workers left in year one, against 12% of comparable hires.[^7] Losses run highest in executive, technical and sales roles, so give those people the new tools first.[^33]
Treating each add-on as easy: announcement returns fall from the fifth deal on, and AI gets little easier per company.[^25][^13] Give every integration its own owner and checklist.
Rolling out with no playbook: 41% of operating partners deploy AI across companies without one.[^5] Prove one playbook at one company, then copy it.

Paying software prices for services firms: automated outsourcing firms trade at 5-23 times operating profit (EBITDA), software at 22-92, per a Fortune commentary.[^34] Price deals on today's cash flow, not promised AI margins.[^9]
Accepting sloppy output: low-quality AI work can wipe out the time saved in services.[^18] Sample output weekly at each company, with a named person signing off.
Pooling customer data carelessly: privacy promises travel with each acquired company.[^28] Map each company's notice before you merge customer lists or train AI on them.

faq.a: A roll-up strategy buys several small companies in one fragmented industry and runs them as one larger business.[^1] It pays when the combined business grows or runs better, not only when it resells at a higher multiple.[^1][^6]

Only some do: 1990s roll-up IPOs lost money on average, while disciplined programmatic acquirers beat peers over a decade.[^22][^2] The gap is operations, and keeping acquired owners involved.[^6][^1]

An AI roll-up is a roll-up, usually venture-funded, that buys services firms and runs them on its own AI software.[^8][^34] Targets include accounting, IT support and property management firms.[^17][^21][^19]

Not proven yet: published results come from the companies or their backers, and investors question the economics.[^8][^9] Our own check of nine public claims found none checked by an outsider.[^19][^17]

faq.q: What is the difference between a serial acquirer and a roll-up?
faq.a: A serial acquirer buys again and again, often keeping companies separate, while a roll-up usually merges them into one platform in one industry.[^23][^1] Serial acquirers were involved in 68% of deals by public acquirers worldwide from 2000 to 2018.[^23]

An independent sponsor buys companies one deal at a time, raising equity for each deal instead of from a committed fund, often from family offices.[^15] In a 2026 survey of 187 sponsor professionals, 79% expect AI to significantly change the model.[^15]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy tools for the jobs every company shares, such as the close, CRM and ticketing.[^35] Most enterprise AI is now bought: 76% of use cases in 2025, up from 53%.[^35] In MIT's study, as Fortune reported, bought tools and partnerships succeeded about 67% of the time, far more often than internal builds.[^36]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only the thin shared layer, such as one data model and group reporting, once several companies use it.[^13] AI roll-ups build whole platforms because the platform is their bet, funded by investors like General Catalyst and Thrive Holdings.[^19][^21] A 40-500 person holdco rarely needs that.

pickElse: You own one PE-backed company, not a group: the cross-company jobs here don't apply yet. Start with that company's first AI job; PE decision-makers say 43% of portfolio companies make no real use of AI yet.[^3]

An enterprise resource planning (ERP) move is coming at your companies anyway: finish it first, since data infrastructure is the top barrier to AI.[^5] Use the AI features in the new system before adding tools.
Your teams only need to write and summarise faster: an enterprise plan of ChatGPT, Claude or Microsoft 365 Copilot will do.[^35]
You are still buying your first company: AI for screening and diligence matters more now. 79% of independent sponsor professionals expect AI to change their model.[^15]

answers.human-role: Your people keep every decision: the holdco CEO owns the AI plan, controllers sign off each close, general managers own pricing, and people decide hiring and pay.[^4][^10][^12]
answers.ranked: AI pays first in shared finance and clean data across companies, then in pricing and cross-sell, then in integrating each new add-on.[^5][^4][^1]
answers.own-data: Little so far: all nine outcome claims we found from four AI roll-ups came from the companies, their backers or partners, none independently checked.[^19][^17][^20][^18]
answers.table-1: Only when they run the companies better: buy-and-builds that relied on resale multiples returned 1.4x, against 2.2x for deals that also grew or lifted margins.[^1] Roll-up initial public offerings (IPOs) of the 1990s lost money on average.[^22][^6]
answers.table-2: Early: 43% of PE portfolio companies make no real use of AI, and only 7% run it at enterprise scale.[^3] In a LATAM survey of 10 operators, 9 had none at closing.[^4]
answers.rules: Merger rules can treat a string of small deals as one, and privacy and hiring rules govern the AI you add.[^27][^28][^12]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI goes wrong in a holdco when key people leave, integrations pile up, results are taken on trust, or customer data is pooled carelessly.[^7][^13][^8][^28]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy standard tools for the close, CRM and ticketing, and build only the thin shared layer, such as one data model and group reporting.[^35][^36]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you own one company rather than a group, an ERP move is coming anyway, or staff only need faster writing.[^3][^5][^35]

offer.heading: Which shared job should your holdco hand to AI first?
offer.body: Start with a job every company shares: the monthly close, data standards or pricing. In 30 minutes we map that job across your companies, with your finance lead and a GM. You leave knowing who signs off at each company and the measure to track.

reviews.notes: Each ranked job now carries one measure the COO can report on (days to close, shared fields, cross-sold revenue, days to report after close). Rewrote two pick-something-else lines that pointed nowhere: the single-company case now says 43% of portfolio companies make no real use of AI yet, and the pre-close case points to screening and diligence.

Spelled out every acronym on first use: PE, LATAM, NIST, CRM, ERP, HSR, FTC, DOJ, IPO, EBITDA, GM. Replaced 'multiple arbitrage' with plain 'reselling at a higher multiple' in the ranked list, table and key numbers. Training row now says onboarding and marketing, matching the survey.

A GM of one acquired company needs to see what stays theirs: pricing and customer changes, and a seat for acquired founders on the rollout group, backed by the roll-up IPO study. The offer now brings a GM into the 30-minute session alongside the finance lead.

Read as the head of finance or controller who runs the group close. Shared finance stays first, links to the multi-entity close guide, and measures days to close and intercompany differences cleared. The controller bullet now says AI drafts matches and flags differences while the controller decides and signs off.

Title is the owner's own question after close, with the main phrase 'roll-up strategy' up front. Bottom line answers in five lines: operations win, companies start near zero, finance and data first, keep acquired people, AI roll-up results are unproven. Description now names independent sponsors, a reader the page serves. Named AI roll-ups appear only as their own cited claims, never ranked.
